Top regulators read riot act over super
TEXT:
The heads of the $2.9 trillion super sector's industry groups have urged Treasury and key regulators at a private meeting to back off on plans to force underperforming super funds to shut down.

Treasury, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission summoned the sector to the "unprecedented" yesterday afternoon meeting in Melbourne.

The AFR Weekend spoke to several players who attended the "tense" discussions where the super sector was read the riot act over an "inertia in reform", in the wake of January's landmark Productivity Commission review.

The meeting, chaired by head of Retirement Income at Treasury Robert Jeremenko with APRA's deputy chair Helen Rowell and ASIC's Danielle Press, was called in the hope of clearing the path for Treasurer Josh Frydenberg to announce a review of the retirement income system and the government's full response to the PC review.

However, key attendees at the meeting including Financial Services Council head Sally Loane, CEO of the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia Martin Fahy, Industry Super Australia CEO Bernie Dean and Eva Scheerlinck from the Australian Institute for Superannuation Trustees, remain at odds. The four agenda items discussed were the allocation of default super, the top 10 "best in show" proposal, an industry expert panel and introducing an annual outcomes test for my MySuper products.

"No one likes the best in show or the expert panel and no one can agree on how to default super but everyone wants to get rid of underperforming funds," one attendee privately said.

But the central focus of the meeting turned to the underlying theme of closing down underperforming funds which has split the sector. Several attendees urged the government to put off the recommendation because of the volume of change working its way through the sector.

The fallback position argued was that APRA needed to be given more time to propose a more detailed methodology on how underperforming funds might be identified, which players might be required to merge and how to deal with issues like impaired assets.

The prudential regulator is proposing later this year to rate super funds as red, amber or green as a mechanism to weed out underperforming funds.

That outcome assessments would cover at least four key areas - net returns, fees and costs, insurance and "sustainability" which will consider fund features such as demographics and inflows versus outflows.

"If you just shout fire and everyone runs for the exits, you need to realise that half the members might get burnt," another attendee said. Before the May federal election, the government deferred its full response to the PC report, partly because it feared a backlash from the powerful superannuation industry that could cost the Coalition votes.

Productivity Commission chairman Michael Brennan recently urged the Morrison government to press ahead with implementing the report's 31 recommendations, which could save consumers $3.8 billion a year. There is also concern among some of the players the changes could force millions into major industry super funds HOST, REST, AustralianSuper and Cbus and wipe out swathes of the retail sector

APRA this week flagged superannuation as one of its four key strategic priorities however insiders have confessed frustration at its limited powers, after APRA's capability review recently found the regulator had dropped the ball on the issue.

The Treasurer has already backed the PC's call for a broader review of the retirement income system, including super, pensions and taxation.

The PC wanted an inquiry to investigate the system before compulsory super is raised from 9.5 per cent of wages to 12 per cent, due to be phased in between 2021 and 2025.

No one likes the best in show or the expert panel and no one can agree on default super.

HEADLINE: Nine delivers shares warning to Macquarie
TEXT:
Nine has warned the Macquarie Media share price could take a hit if its takeover offer is not accepted and no other bidder emerges.

In the Nine bidder's statement released to the market late on Friday afternoon, the media company outlined the reasons why Macquarie shareholders should take the $1.46 per share deal from Nine for the remaining 45.5 per cent of the company it does not already own.

Nine acquired the stake in Macquarie following its $4 billion merger with Fairfax Media, which completed in December last year. Nine owns AFR Weekend.

The document outlined four major reasons for Macquarie shareholders to take the offer: Nine is already Macquarie's majority shareholder, the deal has been recommended by the radio broadcaster's board, the all-cash deal provides certain and immediate value, and investors will no longer be exposed to the risks associated with continued investment in the company.

"Nine ... believes the Offer represents compelling value for your MRN Shares," the statement said. "As an MRN Shareholder, you may be exposed to a number of inherent risks that may affect the market price of the MRN Shares, including, the uncertain future market price of MRN Shares if the Offer is not successful and no alternative proposal emerges.

"There is a risk that the MRN share price may fall if the Offer is not successful and no alternative proposal emerges."

Nine's offer, made earlier in August, was at a major discount to the most recent closing price of $1.745 before the deal became public. Shares closed Friday down 1 per cent to $1.45. The offer gives Macquarie an enterprise value of $275.4 million, including $22 million of debt and its full-year dividend of 2¢ a share.

The offer value is greater than 10 times Macquarie's underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for 2018-19 of $27.1 million.

The deal will largely come down to three shareholders: Nine, ad guru John Singleton and Mark Carnegie. Mr Singleton and Mr Carnegie are expected to back the offer should an independent expert's report being drawn up by PwC conclude the offer is fair and reasonable, or not fair but reasonable.

Mr Singleton stands to make around $81 million from the deal should it go through, while Mr Carnegie would get about $9 million.

A number of small shareholders have come out against the offer, including Wilson Asset Management chairman Geoff Wilson, Centennial Asset Management portfolio manager Matthew Kidman and former radio executive Tim Hughes.

HEADLINE: Debt chasers not worried by jump in court actions
TEXT:
Debt-chasing Collection House has shrugged off concerns that its swarm of bankruptcy actions would turn off flows of debt from big clients such as banks.

The Brisbane-based collection agency on Friday maintained it had always acted appropriately and had not seen institutions cut off access to debt ledgers, which it buys cheaply to reap larger returns.

Collection House was recently revealed to have filed 512 bankruptcy actions in federal courts last year, whereas many rivals were in single or double-digit figures.

It came as Collection House saw net profits rise 17 per cent to $30.7 million, partly fuelled by acquisitions, accounting changes and one-off deals. Earnings per share, which is linked to short-term bonuses, also rose. But its own "normalised" earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation fell 7 per cent to $85.1 million.

A weak performance in its collection services division, which tracks down cash on behalf of big institutions, was linked to disruption from the banking inquiry and the federal election.

Still, the company was upbeat about the future, saying activity had returned to normal and technology was delivering improvements. Shares lifted 11¢ to $1.21 in afternoon trade, but were $1.54 this time last year.

Collection House made headlines this month due to its bankruptcy actions, with several industry sources puzzled by the seemingly high numbers.

The company had, in recent years, flagged it would lower the threshold for taking people to court. But managing director Anthony Rivas on Friday said the higher numbers were partly linked to growth in debt ledgers, and hinted that rivals were taking alternative steps.

He rejected one industry suggestion that automation would have been a factor. "There's a lot of manual review," he said.

He maintained action was taken when people had a high ability but "low willingness" to repay debts.

Collection House chairman Leigh Berkley also said "there are no compliance breaches here … we don't sail close to the wind on any of this."

Institutions such as banks can be highly sensitive to any perception of being tough on consumers, particularly following the royal commission. But Mr Berkley said they had not seen access to bank debt ledgers cut off following the research.

Mr Rivas said Collection House would reduce bankruptcy actions but this had been planned before the headlines. He declined to go into detail, citing commercial confidence.

The overall result was lifted by changes to accounting standards favourably lifting income interest, while the division that purchases debt ledgers posted a revenue rise of 25 per cent to $93.7 million. That was boosted by controversial deals in which Collection House gets upfront cash in exchange for assigning future cash flows from a segment of its debt book.

The division reaping debts on behalf of big institutions saw revenue down 2 per cent to $67.6 million. The banking royal commission was partly blamed. That impact was short term, but Collection House said April's election also bit.

HEADLINE: Missing link in reporting season
TEXT:
Profit reporting season is an ideal opportunity to take the pulse of large Australian businesses and figure out if their boards of directors and senior executives have strategies for dealing with disruption.

This is a really important issue for investors because all the global trends point to the largest companies in Australia being replaced with technology-related stocks over the next couple of decades. Unless, of course, the big and slow-moving incumbents that dominate the S&P ASX200 reinvent themselves.

Reinvention is essential in a business world being disrupted by artificial intelligence, renewable energy, machine learning, data analytics, cloud computing, internet of things, robotics and enhanced community expectations.

It could be risky owning the stocks that become stranded because of the failure of their boards and managers to find a new strategic direction or to build an entirely new business within the confines of the old one.

This trend is already well in train in the United States. There is only one company in the top 10 of the S&P 500 Index that was in the list 20 years ago.

That is Microsoft. It was No. 1 in 1999 with a market cap of $US604 billion and it is No. 1 today with a market cap of $US1 trillion.

As it happens, Microsoft is a glowing case study of a large company that has managed to reinvent itself. Under the creative leadership of Satya Nadella, it is growing at double digits.

The S&P 500's second-largest company in 1999, General Electric, still exists but it is a minnow compared to Microsoft and the other nine top stocks: Apple, Amazon, Google, Facebook, Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, JP Morgan, Johnson & Johnson and Walmart.

GE, which is one-seventh of its size 20 years ago, grew on the back of aggressive expansion in financial services. But the global financial crisis left the company exposed when the tide of liquidity receded.

You would have to say its reinvention from a power equipment company to a diversified industrial and financial services was a failure.

Australia's top 10 companies by market cap are BHP, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Rio Tinto, CSL, Westpac Banking Corp, National Australia Bank, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group, Woolworths, Wesfarmers, Telstra and two resources companies.

You have to go down the list to stock No. 31 to find a technology platform company,which is REA Group. After that it is not until stock No. 43 that you find the global software logistics company WiseTech Global.

If the market valuations of our fast-growing tech stocks continue to expand at the same pace as in 2019, the composition of the top 10 stocks will fundamentally change by 2029.

The profit reporting season gave provided that some large companies with entrenched positions in domestic markets are tentatively moving to disrupt themselves.

But very few companies talked about the creation of disruptive offspring. Perhaps they are wary of the reaction in a market that hates deviation from accepted norms.

Look what happened to Brett Redman at AGL when he said he was going to buy telecommunications provider Vocus for $3 billion. He was quickly put back in his box and the deal was abandoned.

Boards and managers will need to toughen up if they want to get serious about corporate reinvention, whether it involves reshaping the existing business or creating an entirely new one from scratch.

Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy says every business should nurture new businesses either through acquisition or creating start-ups.

Jassy has three questions that sum up the strategic thinking: Is the opportunity big? Is the market well served? Can we do something special or different? Jassy will give an idea the green light if the answers come back as follows: yes, no and yes.

The old-world companies that impressed Chanticleer the most this reporting season because of their strategic response to disruption were: CBA, CSL, Wesfarmers, Telstra, Transurban, Medibank and Qantas.

CBA's relaunch of its banking app and its $US100 million investment in Swedish payments buy-now, pay-later group Klarna showed a management facing into disruption from fintechs.

CSL is in a constant cycle of reinvention. Its shares surged more than any other large-cap stock this reporting season, even though its market cap is $US106 billion.

Chief executive Paul Perreault keeps building new business lines and expanding his product range into areas that disrupt old product lines. CSL is disrupting itself, as it must to survive and prosper.

Wesfarmers has bedded down the purchase of online retailer Catch Group, an acquisition that should help change its culture. CEO Rob Scott is finally getting serious about implementation of digital technology on all the conglomerate's platforms.

The implementation of Microsoft Dynamics365 in the Blackwoods wholesale industrial and safety business is a brilliant case study of using technology to reinvent a business.

Telstra is a quiet achiever. Compare the composition of its revenue now to what it was 20 years, 10 years or even five years ago. Andy Penn is the latest in a line of CEOs who have had to rapidly evolve the telco's business model.

Penn is taking Telstra in the right direction with his formidable commitment to 5G technology, which will be the ultimate platform for the internet of things.

Transurban could easily be mistaken for a toll-road monopolist, a one-trick pony made complacent by its inflation-adjusted toll increases. It is actually evolving into a data analytics company that could develop products tied to smart phones that will be integral to the smooth functioning of every megalopolis.

Medibank under chief executive Craig Drummond is remaking itself from health insurer to healthcare company. Its use of data analytics is industry leading. He is exploring ways to deliver healthcare through the partnership with Nexus hospitals.

Qantas is using its frequent flyer business to help build adjacent businesses in lifestyle and healthcare. CEO Alan Joyce has given the loyalty business the resources and cross-business marketing to create the strongest growth engine inside Qantas. It could grow bigger than the airline.

TONY BOYD

HEADLINE: Water caused tower 'movement'
TEXT:
Evacuations New clue uncovered in ongoing Mascot Towers saga.

Soil-filled water pumped out of Mascot Towers' neighbouring building, Peak Towers, has been identified as the cause of the "movement" in the property that led to its spectacular evacuation on June 14, the latest strata documents show.

Exclusive documents obtained by AFR Weekend reveal the outcome of the two-month investigation at the building in Sydney's Mascot, as well as the history of original construction defects which were not related to the recent "cracks" and evacuation.

A geotechnical engineer hired by Mascot Towers, who inspected Peak Towers at 27 Church Street in Mascot 10 days ago, "observed that the property was pumping soil-filled water from under the building".

He said the pumping was contributing to the settlement, or movement, in the building and recommended it should stop.

The discovery was made three days before owners approved the raising of a special levy of $7.7 million to start first-stage remediation of the building.

The owners' lawyers, Grace Lawyers, urged owners to act quickly to "protect the building and its rights against the parties involved in the construction of 27 Church Street".

"Preliminary views are that the adjoining property at 27 Church Street may (in all probability) be the cause of the settlement/cracking that eventuated in the evacuation of the building," Grace Lawyers said in strata documents. The lawyers have asked owners to approve an injunction to stop the pumping and order access into Peak Towers for further inspections.

They also advised owners to commence "urgent" legal action against the building, which was completed in June just as Mascot Towers was evacuated.

The developer and builder of Peak Towers, Aland, told the Financial Review it was not unusual for buildings constructed in a "water table" area like Mascot to experience some level of seepage after construction and it would work with the new owners of Peak Towers and Bayside Council to ensure compliance.

"Aland's Peak Towers has been designed and constructed to meet all building and engineering standards," Aland managing director Andrew Hrsto said.

"With regards to Mascot Towers, Aland has offered to assist the formal government inquiry into the building's longstanding structural issues, and recently invited the NSW building commissioner to inspect Peak Towers as part of his role.

"We are not going to comment on speculation unrelated to the formal investigation."

Aland maintained it was not responsible for Mascot Towers' damages and lodged with Bayside Council a dilapidation report on existing defects at the building, which described it as being in "a reasonable to poor condition".

"The exterior of the building was in a reasonable condition with some cases of cracking and material loss through the walls and undersides as well as separation through the pavement and undersides," the report said.

Crucially, Mascot Towers' engineers said the cracks and movements that resulted in evacuation were "unrelated to any construction defects" within the building. These existing defects - which Aland has cited in its dilapidation report - were allegedly a result of the original construction of the building by the developer and builder J&B Elias Pty Ltd. The company denies any wrongdoing.

The new NSW building commissioner David Chandler said the engineer's new findings were a matter for Mascot Towers, its lawyers and insurers. He cautioned that before any action was taken, a peer review of the findings at Mascot Towers should be undertaken.

HEADLINE: We can balance the great powers
TEXT:
Global perspective Neither the US nor China can dominate the other. That makes the world a lot safer for smart middle powers that know their own strengths.

"Speak softly and carry a big stick, you will go far," US president Theodore Roosevelt was fond of saying. The idea is to negotiate peacefully but also have strength in case things go wrong. Few could disagree that China's rise has uncertain implications for war and peace in the 21st century.

However, fears that Australia is unprepared to defend itself - or too soft - against an all-powerful China may do more harm than good. Prudent internationalism is in fact realpolitik born of our strengths and China's weaknesses.

Any realist foreign policy begins by recognising the limits of what is feasible and what is desirable. There are three trends that emerge from my research on the Asia Power Index that are set to shape the region in decades to come.

First, under most scenarios, the United States will not be able to halt the narrowing power differential between itself and China. Nor, however, will Beijing simply grab the sceptre of unipolarity off the Americans. It is increasingly likely that neither power will be able to exert undisputed primacy in our region. China is a formidable military power and has weaponry that could assail US and allied bases in the region. However, that the superpowers appear equally vulnerable in Asia may paradoxically lower the risk of a full-blown war and, for now at least, push great power rivalry below the threshold of conflict.

Second, globalisation will still involve the US and China, even if the two become less dependent on each other. China is too enmeshed in the international system to be contained. There are fewer ideological compulsions and economic advantage counts for more than during the last cold war. Rather than choosing sides, China pushback from countries in the region will be issue-specific, and reflect varying national interest calculations.

Third, far from being the hapless victims, middle powers will become more important in an age of great power competition. When two superpowers are gridlocked, the actions of the next rung of powers will constitute the marginal difference. Australia is more than capable of forging a favourable - and preferably peaceful - balance of power in the region, one that balances the sharpening ambitions of China. What is needed is a more sober articulation of the challenges confronting us.

Liberal MP Andrew Hastie recently placed Australia's failure to take stock of China's "mobile authoritarianism" on an equal footing to the failure of the French to contain German expansionism in 1940. Proponents of this school of thought are setting wheels in motion to act in a way that any cool assessment of China would advise against. It leads to a distorted view of our vulnerabilities and falsely equates prudent diplomacy with strategic apathy.

We are stronger than we give ourselves credit for. Roosevelt described his mantra as "the exercise of intelligent forethought and of decisive action sufficiently far in advance of any likely crisis". Our response to foreign influence offers a case in point. Australia's democratic institutions have shown themselves capable of recognising and addressing foreign influence before it becomes an insurmountable threat.

A better historical analogy might be that Australia is operationalising its own version of the Monroe Doctrine in mounting a Pacific "step-up" to ensure we remain the partner of choice in our near abroad. Building a joint military base with the US on Manus Island will maximise the defensive advantages of Australia's first island chain.

If there is a flaw in our strategy, however, it is that our fixation on great power rivalry comes at the expense of other issues of concern to our Pacific neighbours. Without Australian leadership on climate change, economic cooperation and inequality, China's overtures on these issues will find greater traction. That would be ironic, given China's pollution, protectionism and economic disparities at home.

Any policy recalibration also entails the risk of overcorrection. The Trump administration's trade wars, for example, may cause irreversible damage to the rules-based trading system, not fix it. That would result in a world where size and economic power, not principles or rules, dictate the terms of engagement. Such a system will hurt smaller countries and likely favour China.

It would be equally mistaken to present our efforts as a struggle between Eastern totalitarian and Western democratic blocs. Not when the coalition we must assemble will have to encompass a broad church of political systems.

We can be quietly confident that if we premise our foreign policy on pragmatic overlapping interests that China's power will remain hobbled - not least due to a lack of trust among 11 of its neighbours with which it has boundary disputes or legacies of interstate conflict.

As China's presence in contested spaces grows, so too do efforts to create a military and strategic counterweight in response.

At the same time, a parochial, ethnocentric brand of authoritarian nationalism is not proving a particularly exportable ideology. In fact, President Xi Jinping's authoritarian lurch betrays weakness as much as strength. The one-party state spends more on projecting power inwards, on internal security, than it does on projecting it outwards, on military spending.

We might learn from the strategic cultures of other middle powers with an interest in balancing China. Japan and Vietnam, for example, have far more proximate causes to fear China. Yet they have perfected the art of sizing up China correctly, balancing engagement with confrontation.

Carrying a big stick whilst privileging diplomacy and middle power cooperation is the only hard-headed approach to challenging and co-existing with an authoritarian China in a globalised system.

Herve Lemahieu is director of the Asian Power and Diplomacy Program at the Lowy Institute.
